title: Lawyers in your living room! : law on television
finding: Edited volume (Asimow ed.) covering US legal series from Perry Mason to Law & Order; per the editor, most members of the public receive most of their information and misinformation about what lawyers and judges do from TV portrayals.
why_for_us: Legal TV is a primary source of 'how law works' for laypeople; for a notary audience the opposite applies - they will check every procedural detail, so the notary sign-off on each episode is not optional.

title: Lawyers and the legal system on TV: the British experience
venue: International Journal of Law in Context
finding: Essay surveying how British TV portrays lawyers and the legal system in the wake of US output, tracing changes in small-screen lawyer portrayals and building on US scholarship.
why_for_us: Shows that national legal systems get filtered through US genre templates; a Polish notary series should avoid importing courtroom-lawyer tropes that do not exist in notarial practice.

title: The Treatment of the Law: Between Reality and Imagination in Television Legal Series
finding: Essay arguing that as US legal series grew more complex, details of courtroom set-up and what lawyers may or may not do became increasingly precise, while some elements were deliberately stretched to engender curiosity.
why_for_us: Supports a model of 'precise core, stretched periphery': keep the notarial act, documents and duties exact; dramatise only pacing, emotion and stakes.

title: Taking L. A. Law More Seriously
finding: Law-review essay by a legal-ethics scholar arguing that L.A. Law's appeal rests on combining glossy 'L.A.' drama with real legal substance, and that the substance part deserves serious attention.
why_for_us: Professionals tolerate gloss if the legal substance is real; a 60-90 s episode can be stylish provided the legal point is correct and recognisable.

title: Mirrors In the Robing Room: Reflections of Lawyers and the Law In Canadian Television Drama
venue: Canadian Journal of Law and Society
finding: Analysis of CBC series and legal docudramas showing that national TV 'inflects' genre formula in distinctive ways; it closes with lawyers' reactions to their own television image.
why_for_us: A local (non-US) legal drama can build its own formula; lawyers' reactions to their screen image are a test audience worth piloting with notaries before release.

title: PRIME-TIME CRIME: PRESENTATIONS OF CRIME AND ITS PARTICIPANTS ON POPULAR TELEVISION JUSTICE PROGRAMS
finding: Content analysis of Law and Order, The Practice and NYPD Blue found an overrepresentation of violent crime and distorted images of offenders and victims, confirming earlier studies.
why_for_us: Mainstream justice TV systematically distorts the case mix; a notary series built on documented cases can differentiate itself by showing the real, mostly non-violent, fraud and document cases notaries meet.

title: Crime-Show-Viewing Habits and Public Attitudes Toward Forensic Evidence: The “CSI Effect” Revisited
finding: Telephone survey of a random sample of 1,201 California registered voters: per authors, crime-show viewing predicted pretrial attitudes toward scientific evidence and testimony independently of background, and had a direct effect on stated willingness to convict/acquit depending on forensic evidence.
why_for_us: Fiction shapes what people expect evidence to look like; showing a notary verifying identity and documents the real way can recalibrate expectations instead of feeding a 'magic tech' myth.

title: Beyond Frequency: Perceived Realism and the CSI Effect
venue: Canadian Journal of Criminology and Criminal Justice
finding: Mock-juror study with a DNA-evidence trial transcript: per authors, both viewing frequency and perceived realism of crime TV had direct and indirect effects on information processing, attitudes and decisions.
why_for_us: Effects depend on how realistic viewers believe a show is; high perceived realism among notaries makes accuracy both a credibility asset and a responsibility.

title: The CSI Effect and the Canadian and the Australian Jury
finding: Survey of 605 Canadian jury-eligible students plus surveys/interviews of real Australian post-trial jurors: viewing habits influenced treatment of some forensic evidence, but no support was found for a detrimental CSI effect; Australian jurors assessed forensic evidence in a balanced way.
why_for_us: Real decision-makers are more sober than the moral panic suggests; the series can portray AI as a careful aid, not as an infallible oracle, without fear of being 'boring'.

title: INVESTIGATING THE 'CSI EFFECT' EFFECT: MEDIA AND LITIGATION CRISIS IN CRIMINAL LAW
finding: Analysis of actual acquittal rates in state criminal trials found only equivocal evidence of change after CSI, while a content analysis of media claims showed the press presented the CSI effect as real despite little supporting evidence.
why_for_us: Claims about media effects on legal professionals are often folklore; marketing copy should not promise that the series 'changes how notaries work' without our own measurement.

title: Viewing CSI and the Threshold of Guilt: Managing Truth and Justice in Reality and Fiction
finding: Review essay arguing that existing evidence is equally consistent with CSI making jurors more likely to convict as to acquit, that perceived acquittal rises can be explained without CSI, and that legal reform based on the untested effect is premature.
why_for_us: A reminder that fiction's influence on legal actors is plausible but unproven in direction; show AI in a way whose possible over-trust effect is benign (prompting verification, not replacing it).

title: Watching the Detectives: Crime Programming, Fear of Crime, and Attitudes about the Criminal Justice System
finding: Survey analysis: fear mediated the link between viewing nonfictional crime shows and lower support for the justice system; crime-drama viewing predicted support for the death penalty without mediation by fear; news viewing was unrelated.
why_for_us: Genre matters: reality-style crime content erodes trust, fictional crime drama pushes punitiveness; a notary series based on real cases should keep a reassuring, institution-affirming resolution.

title: Does Watching Court TV `Cultivate' People's Perceptions of Crime?
finding: Questionnaire of 305 adults near Boston and New York identified five Court TV viewing motives (voyeurism, boredom-avoidance, entertainment, relaxation, information); entertainment was most prominent; heavier and information-motivated viewers held more negative perceptions of crime.
why_for_us: Even 'real' court content is watched mainly for entertainment and voyeurism; the series can openly be entertainment while keeping the information layer correct.

title: The Effects of United States Television Programs upon Canadian Beliefs about Legal Procedure
finding: Study of whether incidental learning from US programs such as Perry Mason led Canadian viewers to hold false beliefs about their own courtroom procedure (abstract states the concern; results not given in the record).
why_for_us: Early evidence base for 'foreign-system leakage'; Polish viewers likewise may hold US-derived beliefs about procedure that a notary series can gently correct.

title: Media Coverage of Law: Its Impact on Juries and the Public
finding: Review: because most people have little direct experience with the justice system, their knowledge and views of law depend largely on media; TV news and police/crime dramas account for much incidental learning about law.
why_for_us: Notaries' clients learn law from screens; episodes can double as client-expectation management content for notary offices.

title: From Judge Judy to Judge Rinder and Judge Geordie: humour, emotion and ‘televisual legal consciousness’
venue: International Journal of Law in Context
finding: Analysis of two British court TV shows argues they should be read as television, not compared with real courts: Judge Rinder's daytime address and camped authority let humour disarm conflict, creating a 'televisual legal consciousness'.
why_for_us: Humour and a strong authority figure can carry legal content without undermining it; a notary protagonist can be warm and witty while remaining the authority.

title: Legal series and legal careers: Investigating relationships between watching the legal drama Suits and law school enrollment
finding: Logistic regressions on data from 1,353 students in Münster, Germany: per author, watching legal series was highly significantly related to studying law, and the broadcasting of Suits was followed by a rise in applications and enrollment at Münster Law School.
why_for_us: Legal series attract people to legal professions even in a civil-law country; a notary series could also serve recruitment of staff (aplikanci, assistants), not only SaaS sales.

title: ‘Represent a murderer… I’d never do that!’ How students use stories to link ethical development and identity construction
finding: Chapter arguing that first-year law students use TV lawyer images to identify positive and negative aspects of lawyering, showing both a lack of ethical knowledge and a substantial capacity for ethical reflection when discussing fictional law stories.
why_for_us: Short fiction works as an ethics prompt; each episode can end on a recognisable professional-duty dilemma that staff can discuss.

title: A vigilante serial killer as ethics educator? An exploration of Dexter as a tool for moral education in the professional domain
finding: In-depth interviews (N = 61) with law and psychology students: law students initially followed Dexter's unlawful reasoning but slowly developed a strict procedural viewpoint during education; authors recommend using such dramas later in the curriculum.
why_for_us: Experienced legal professionals judge fiction procedurally; for notaries, outcome-over-rules shortcuts by the hero will read as wrong, so the notary must win by the rules.

title: Teaching professional ethics through popular culture
finding: Reflective account of a UK law-school course teaching professional ethics through popular culture, responding to the LETR call to strengthen ethics education.
why_for_us: Popular-culture ethics teaching is an accepted method; episodes could be packaged for notarial chamber training sessions.

title: Film and literature in the legal classroom
finding: Essay describing growing use of legal-themed films and literature in law schools to examine lawyer skills (argument, negotiation, advocacy), the legal process and legal-ethical theory.
why_for_us: Supports a 'skills on display' angle: show the notary's concrete skills (explaining, verifying, refusing) rather than abstract virtue.

title: REEL TO REAL: USING FILM REFLECTIONS TO CULTIVATE CRITICAL THINKING IN PROFESSIONAL ETHICS EDUCATION
finding: Final-year Malaysian law students analysed ethical dilemmas in films against the Legal Profession Act and Bar rules; themes were judicial-process integrity and professional independence; survey showed high perceived relevance (mean 9.31/10) and preference for film-based assessment.
why_for_us: Legal learners value fiction when they can map it onto actual rules; each episode could cite the real provision (e.g. Prawo o notariacie) in a caption.

title: Diventare avvocati e riuscire ad esserlo: insegnare l'etica delle professioni forensi attraverso le trame narrative
venue: Unitn Eprints Research (Università Degli Studi di Trento)
finding: Italian essay structuring lawyering as knowing, knowing-how and knowing-how-to-be, arguing the last (professional identity and ethics) is best taught through narrative plots.
why_for_us: A civil-law source endorsing stories as the vehicle for professional identity; supports framing the series as identity content for notarial staff.

title: Undisclosed Information— Serial Is My Favorite Murder: Examining Motivations in the True Crime Podcast Audience
finding: Online survey (n = 308): true crime podcast audience was 73% female; top motivations were entertainment, convenience and boredom; social interaction, escape and voyeurism were significantly more salient for women.
why_for_us: Notary office staff are largely women; true-crime-style real cases with a social, discussable angle fit this audience's motives.

title: Captured by True Crime: Why Are Women Drawn to Tales of Rape, Murder, and Serial Killers?
finding: Five studies (reader reviews, book choices, manipulated story features): women were more drawn to true crime than men, who preferred other violent genres; manipulations identified story features women find appealing, interpreted in evolutionary terms.
why_for_us: Real-crime content appeals to women partly for its protective/learning value; fraud-prevention cases where the notary protects a vulnerable client fit that pull.

title: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime
finding: Behavioural investigation (n = 307-571) confirmed a robust gender difference favouring women, found general (morbid curiosity) and distinct motives (defensive vigilance, excitement); gender, income, fear of crime and antagonism predicted consumption; defensive vigilance (higher in women) was linked to adaptive self-regulation.
why_for_us: 'Defensive vigilance' is the motive to target: episodes that teach how to spot a forged power of attorney or identity fraud give staff a usable protective lesson.

title: Positive and negative perceptions of true crime podcasts: surveying female, male, and nonbinary listeners
finding: Survey of true crime podcast listeners: most common motivations were entertainment and multitasking; female and nonbinary participants more often listened for safety reasons and reported more fear of crime since listening.
why_for_us: Real-case content can raise fear; endings should restore control (fraud stopped, procedure worked) rather than leave anxiety.

title: True Crime Podcasts in Australia: Examining Listening Patterns and Listener Perceptions
finding: Survey of 124 university students on true crime podcast subject matter, listening patterns, stylistic attributes, motivations and perceptions; authors stress the public may treat such podcasts as authoritative resources on crime.
why_for_us: Audiences treat real-case content as authoritative; any factual error in a case-based episode will be read as a claim about reality, raising the accuracy bar.

title: “It’s that ‘There but for the Grace of God Go I’ Piece of It”: Domestic Violence Survivors in True Crime Podcast Audiences
finding: Qualitative interviews with 16 women who are domestic-violence survivors and true crime fans: they were drawn by audio appeal, the power of a good story, educational value, therapeutic understanding and community camaraderie.
why_for_us: Educational value and community are core gratifications; episodes should carry one practical takeaway and invite comments from notary staff.

title: Cold case comfort: Emotions, motivations, and identities of true crime fans
finding: In-depth interviews with true crime consumers and creators reaffirm therapeutic and justice-oriented motives and propose 'repair work' (internal healing and external pro-social action) as a unifying framework.
why_for_us: Justice-oriented, pro-social real cases (the notary prevents harm) align with what true crime fans say they get from the genre.

title: Fenomen podkastów „true crime”. Przypis do historii medializacji przemocy
finding: Polish essay on true crime podcasts and their audience, comparing the genre with traditional crime fiction and linking audience motives to civilisational change in instincts and inner imperatives.
why_for_us: The only Polish-language true crime audience source found; confirms the genre is discussed in Poland but offers no empirical numbers.

title: Creating Law Franchises on Television
finding: Essay by the writer/producer of major US legal shows arguing legal franchises keep thriving because they evolve like the law and are intellectually challenging and emotionally appealing.
why_for_us: Practitioner view that intellectual challenge is part of the pleasure; give the notary audience a small legal puzzle they can solve before the reveal.

title: Use of a Television Crime-Drama Series to Promote Legal Understanding in Mentally Ill, Incompetent Defendants: A Pilot Study
finding: Pilot study (N = 15) of a competency-restoration programme that used videotaped Law & Order segments among other techniques to promote understanding of trial competency in incompetent defendants.
why_for_us: Dramatised procedure can teach procedure; short episodes can be designed to leave one accurate procedural step in memory.

title: Aesthetic Cognitivism and Serialized Television Fiction
venue: Journal of Aesthetics and Art Criticism
finding: Philosophical article defending the cognitive value of generic TV series, focusing on crime and related genres as sources of understanding of social reality.
why_for_us: Theoretical backing for 'learning how institutions work' as a legitimate pleasure of procedural fiction.

title: Confined, Crammed, and Inextricable: What the Wire Gets Rights
finding: Essay by a criminal-procedure professor arguing The Wire's appeal to law teachers lies less in obvious realism than in showing, in grim detail, how the justice system goes wrong.
why_for_us: Legal professionals enjoy fiction that shows system mechanics truthfully, including failure modes; episodes can show where procedure catches fraud and where it nearly fails.

title: Enjoyment of films as a function of narrative experience, perceived realism and transportability
finding: Survey across three films of different genres: transportability, external realism (match to the world) and narrative realism (story coherence) each positively influenced at least one aspect of narrative experience, which in turn predicted enjoyment.
why_for_us: Realism is not only a duty but a driver of enjoyment; for notaries, external realism (correct procedure) and narrative coherence both feed liking.

title: “I Really Liked That Movie”: Testing the Relationship Between Trait Empathy, Transportation, Perceived Realism, and Movie Enjoyment
finding: Undergraduates (N = 199) evaluated two recently seen films: fantasy empathy was associated with transportation, and transportation was linked to film enjoyment alongside perceived realism.
why_for_us: Empathy and transportation drive liking; even 60-90 s episodes need a character to feel for (client, assistant), not just a legal point.

title: Moral Judgment and Crime Drama: An Integrated Theory of Enjoyment
finding: Theory paper combining moral reasoning about mediated crime and punishment with affective disposition theory: crime dramas function as statements about justice, and viewers' moral deliberation about those statements shapes enjoyment.
why_for_us: Enjoyment of a case story depends on viewers approving of how justice is served; the notary's resolution must feel just to notaries, not only legally valid.

title: Moral Judgment as a Predictor of Enjoyment of Crime Drama
finding: Experiment (N = 139) with two crime-punishment film clips differing in crime type: enjoyment levels were similar, but were predicted by different moral-judgment factors in each condition, supporting disposition theory.
why_for_us: Different kinds of wrongdoing activate different moral criteria; fraud against elderly clients vs. tax tricks will be judged differently, so the 'right' outcome must be matched to the case type.

title: Punishing Media Criminals and Moral Judgment: The Impact on Enjoyment
finding: Experiment (N = 151) varying punishment of a perpetrator (excessive vs. none): enjoyment was consistently predicted by social-justice attitudes and resulting moral judgments about the content.
why_for_us: Over- or under-punishment both risk the audience; a proportionate, procedural consequence (refusal, report, annulment) is the safest payoff.

title: A Just and Happy Ending: Exploring Viewers’ Judgment of Justice on Enjoyment of Crime Drama in Interactive Movie Events
finding: Lab experiment (N = 148) with a full interactive movie manipulating viewers' notion of what is just versus what is shown: enjoyment was a function of viewers' judgment of justice, and virtually present co-viewers acted as a 'justice compass'.
why_for_us: Comment sections act as co-viewers; seeding notary community discussion may steer how justly an episode is perceived.

title: The Double Meaning of Law: Does it Matter if Film Lawyers are Unethical?
venue: Oxford University Press eBooks (Law and Popular Culture)
finding: Chapter examining how film lawyers depart from professional conduct codes to achieve what they see as justice, arguing that these ethical departures let audiences engage with complex characters.
why_for_us: General audiences enjoy rule-bending lawyers, but the canon (notary-authorised, no errors) excludes it; tension must come from external pressure, not from the notary breaking rules.

title: Is There an Honest Lawyer in the Box? Legal Ethics on TV
finding: Book chapter surveying lawyers' ethical dilemmas, choices and violations on US TV from Perry Mason to Boston Legal, with themes of generational learning and collegial support.
why_for_us: Collegial support and mentor-apprentice learning are recurring ethical themes; a notary-assistant pair fits this established pattern.

title: Procedural Unfairness in Real and Film Trials: Why do Audiences Understand Stories Placed in Foreign Legal Systems?
venue: Oxford University Press eBooks (Law and Popular Culture)
finding: Chapter arguing that law films travel across legal systems because audiences evaluate legal institutions and actors by basic standards of procedural fairness, which matter more than system-specific rules.
why_for_us: Fairness is the universal hook; notarial stories can be gripping to lay viewers if the drama turns on fairness to a vulnerable party, even when details are civil-law specific.

title: Law in Film: Globalizing the Hollywood Courtroom Drama
finding: Essay asking why even films set in continental Europe follow US courtroom-drama patterns and repeat American elements, noting these films strongly shape public concepts of justice although few reflect legal reality.
why_for_us: Polish audiences carry US courtroom templates; a notary series should deliberately avoid 'objection!'-style tropes and make the civil-law setting part of its novelty.

title: Recht im Film: Abbild juristischer Wirklichkeit oder filmische Selbstreferenz?
finding: German essay: American films have influenced German audiences' thinking about law and justice; even legal films set in Germany follow American patterns; discusses why the US criminal trial is so attractive and how courtroom dramas can be used in university teaching.
why_for_us: Direct civil-law evidence of US-template dominance; the series has a niche in authentic continental procedure.

title: Deterred from going to court? A survey at German schools on media influences
finding: Survey of 12th-grade students at German technical colleges and high schools: media effects on attitudes to going to lawyers and courts occur but are modest, against a background of rather high trust in courts and the legal profession in Germany.
why_for_us: In civil-law countries with high baseline trust, fiction nudges rather than shapes; the series should reinforce existing trust in notaries rather than try to rebuild it.

title: Polish Contemporary Legal System in Court Shows and Courtroom Dramas
venue: Law and Administration in Post-Soviet Europe
finding: Article on how the Polish legal system is depicted in Polish court shows and courtroom dramas (record keywords cite e.g. 'Prawo Agaty'); the OpenAlex record carries no usable abstract.
why_for_us: The only indexed study of Polish legal TV found; should be read in full before writing, to know which Polish tropes notaries have already seen.

title: When law goes pop - teaching Legal English through TV courtroom shows
finding: Teaching report from Warsaw: law students admitted watching 'Sędzia Anna Maria Wesołowska' and found it resembled real proceedings, whereas legal trainees and practitioners vehemently rejected such shows as distorting real justice.
why_for_us: Direct Polish evidence that practising lawyers reject TV-style legal distortions; the notary audience will punish any 'Wesołowska-style' shortcut.

title: Justices à l'écran
finding: Book by a French judge: the French too often believe their justice resembles what they see on screen, where Anglo-Saxon justice dominates; explores accusatorial vs. inquisitorial differences through major films.
why_for_us: Same misconception exists in other civil-law countries; a short caption contrasting 'what TV shows vs. what the notary actually does' can be a recurring device.

title: À l’école des séries judiciaires : la fiction au service de la représentation télévisuelle de l’avocat et de la justice aux États-Unis et en France
finding: Essay: legal series give easy access to reference points about justice and the professions in an entertainment context that favours acquisition of legal culture; US series, often written by mixed teams including lawyers, have projected a positive image of the defence lawyer for sixty years.
why_for_us: Mixed writer-lawyer teams are the norm behind credible legal series; formalise the authorising notary as a co-writer credit.

title: Television and the Legal System
finding: Book tracing the US TV legal series as a source of legal information and myth, contrasting it with France, where interest in legal series is similar but representations of justice differ strikingly.
why_for_us: Comparative US-France evidence that civil-law fiction needs its own representational codes; useful model for a Polish notarial genre.

title: The portrayal of law in the movie
venue: Digital Repository (National Repository of Grey Literature, Charles University)
finding: Czech diploma thesis analysing the TV show 'Judge Barbara' (Sédzia Barbara): the means used to capture the judicial environment, viewers' impressions, comparison with reality and the show's educational potential.
why_for_us: Closest analogue to Polish court TV in a neighbouring civil-law country; thesis-level only.

title: The Influence of Paratext on Narrative Persuasion: Fact, Fiction, or Fake?
finding: Study 1 (N = 135): stories introduced as nonfiction were expected to be more trustworthy/useful, fiction more immersive. Study 2 (experiment, N = 186): the story persuaded in nonfiction, fiction and fake conditions; need for cognition increased the nonfiction-vs-fake gap; fiction beat fake via deeper transportation.
why_for_us: A 'based on a real case' label raises perceived usefulness for notaries but does not by itself make the story more persuasive; the case must also be well told.

title: When Fiction Is Just as Real as Fact: No Differences in Reading Behavior between Stories Believed to be Based on True or Fictional Events
finding: Online experiment (final N = 1,742): labelling a story as based on true events or as fictional had no detectable effect on immersion, appreciation, perspective taking or memory; narrative perspective partly mattered.
why_for_us: Do not rely on the 'true case' label for engagement; its value for us is credibility and the authorising notary's comfort, not immersion.

title: Fact Versus Fiction Labeling: Persuasion Parity Despite Heightened Scrutiny of Fact
finding: Two experiments (392 students): a 'fact' label enhanced critical scrutiny among low need-for-cognition readers when relevance was unspecified or low; high-NC readers scrutinised regardless; fact-labelled communications were no more persuasive than fiction-labelled ones.
why_for_us: Labelling episodes as real cases invites scrutiny; notaries (high-NC, high relevance) will scrutinise anyway, so every fact in a case-based episode must survive checking.

title: Amazing but true: A preference for fiction-like non-fiction
finding: Three studies (synopses, website vignettes, narratives): readers preferred stories presented externally as non-fiction but written internally like fiction, and relied more on factual stories to update notions of reality.
why_for_us: Best of both: present episodes as real documented cases but tell them with fiction craft (hook, twist, payoff).

title: Emotions Bias Perceptions of Realism in Audiovisual Media: Why We May Take Fiction for Real
finding: Two experiments manipulating mood and framing of a TV documentary as fiction- vs reality-based: emotional viewers attributed more realism and information value to the programme believed fictional; empathy increased perceived realism and information value.
why_for_us: Emotional engagement inflates perceived realism; with real-case framing this raises responsibility to keep emotionally charged scenes factually exact.

title: Does Perceived Realism Really Matter in Media Effects?
finding: Experiment with adults: documentary excerpts were perceived as more factual, but memory for visual/verbal information and emotional intensity were greater for fiction excerpts; perceived factuality influenced adults less than younger viewers.
why_for_us: Fiction craft beats documentary form for memory and emotion; a dramatised reconstruction of a real case is likely to be remembered better than a factual summary.
